title: Mastery Challenge: Logic & Critical Thinking
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Logic & Critical Thinking Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: arguments, hidden premises, explanations, and deciding and thinking clearly. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Logic & Critical Thinking Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from what an argument is to how to decide and think clearly. Level 1 asked whether dark windows really mean a café is closed; now see how far that one question reaches. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Logic & Critical Thinking: mastered
learned: How to take any argument apart into claims, premises, hidden assumptions and conclusion.
Why a bad argument does not make its conclusion false, and why you can prove a negative.
How to judge a decision by what was known at the time, and ignore costs already sunk.
Why belief should move in proportion to evidence, and how to face the strongest opposing view.

questions.prompt: A friend says an argument in logic means two people disagreeing loudly. What is the best correction?

options.label: It means claims offered as reasons for another claim
It means a debate with a judge and a winner
options.rationale: Nobody needs to win for there to be an argument.

options.label: It means any statement said with strong feeling
options.rationale: A heated assertion is not an argument.

options.label: It means two people contradicting each other
options.rationale: That's a quarrel, the everyday sense.

questions.explanation: In logic, an argument is a set of statements, some offered as reasons for thinking another is true.

questions.prompt: "The shop is shut, so it must be a holiday." Which unstated premise would make this work?

options.label: Holidays are good for business
options.rationale: That doesn't link shut to holiday.

options.label: The shop shuts only on holidays
Everyone likes a holiday
options.rationale: A taste claim does not help the argument.

options.label: Shops should open every day
options.rationale: A value judgment doesn't connect the claims.

questions.explanation: Ask what else must be true for the conclusion to follow: the shop shuts only on holidays.

questions.prompt: Looking at a flooded kitchen, a plumber says: "The pipe burst because the water in it froze." What is she giving?

options.label: An argument that the pipe burst
options.rationale: Nobody doubts it burst; the water is on the floor.

options.label: A value judgment about the pipe
options.rationale: She says what happened, not what should.

options.label: An explanation of why it burst
A question about the weather
options.rationale: It's a claim, not a question.

questions.explanation: The burst is already accepted, so the "because" explains why it happened rather than arguing that it did.

questions.prompt: A coach's sensible game plan loses to a lucky last-second shot. Calling the plan bad for that reason is which error?

options.label: The sunk cost trap
options.rationale: That's about letting past spending steer the next choice.

options.label: The fallacy fallacy
options.rationale: That's rejecting a conclusion because its argument was bad.

options.label: Miscalibration
options.rationale: That's confidence not matching your record.

options.label: Outcome bias

questions.explanation: Outcome bias judges a decision by how it turned out instead of by what was known when it was made.

questions.prompt: A company has spent a year building an app that is failing. Which reason for continuing is sound?

options.label: We have already spent a year on it
options.rationale: That's the sunk cost: spent either way.

options.label: Finishing will bring in more than it costs from here
Stopping now would mean admitting a mistake
options.rationale: That's the pull of the sunk cost, not a reason.

options.label: The money is wasted unless we finish
options.rationale: The money is spent whether they finish or not.

questions.explanation: Only future costs and benefits differ between the options. The year already spent is sunk.

questions.prompt: Which method starts by imagining a plan has already failed, to find its weak points in time?

options.label: A post-mortem
options.rationale: That comes after a real failure, too late to fix the plan.

options.label: A steel man
options.rationale: That's the strongest version of an opposing view.

options.label: A pre-mortem
Calibration
options.rationale: That's matching your confidence to your record.

questions.explanation: Gary Klein's pre-mortem assumes the project has failed and asks what went wrong, while the plan can still change.

questions.prompt: Ana is "totally sure" of most of her guesses, yet many turn out wrong. What is she short of?

options.label: Calibration: confidence that matches her record
Confidence: she needs to feel even surer
options.rationale: More sureness would make the mismatch worse.

options.label: Charity: she needs to fill gaps generously
options.rationale: Charity is for rebuilding others' arguments.

options.label: Foresight: she needs to predict more often
options.rationale: The problem is how sure she is, not how often she predicts.

questions.explanation: Her confidence runs well ahead of how often she is right: she is overconfident, so poorly calibrated.

questions.prompt: Ten reliable neighbors report the same lost cat on your street. By Hume's rule, how should your belief in the lost cat shift?

options.label: Not at all, until you see the cat yourself
options.rationale: Ignoring strong evidence is too little.

options.label: Only a tiny amount, like one rumor would
options.rationale: Many reliable reports are strong evidence.

options.label: Only if a newspaper confirms it
options.rationale: Good evidence already exists.

options.label: A long way, since the evidence is strong

questions.explanation: Proportion belief to the evidence: many independent, reliable reports should turn the dial a long way.

questions.prompt: Before criticizing your neighbor's plan for the garden, you restate it so well she says, "Yes, exactly." What have you built?

options.label: A straw man
options.rationale: A straw man is a weakened version, easy to knock down.

options.label: A steel man
An unstated premise
options.rationale: You restated her whole view, not one hidden part of it.

options.label: A pre-mortem
options.rationale: You didn't imagine the garden failing.

questions.explanation: You've built the other view at its strongest, in a form its believer accepts: a steel man.

questions.prompt: You spot a fallacy in a friend's argument for a claim. What have you shown about the claim itself?

options.label: That the claim is false
options.rationale: That's the fallacy fallacy.

options.label: That the claim is true after all
options.rationale: A fallacy tells you nothing either way about the claim.

options.label: Only that this argument doesn't support it
That your friend cannot be trusted
options.rationale: That's an attack on the arguer, not the claim.

questions.explanation: A fallacious argument fails to support its conclusion. The claim may still be true for other reasons.
